extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patentees, and courts (UK practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on criteria and procedural requirements for patent extension applications, revocation petitions, particulars in infringement actions, interlocutory and perpetual injunctions, inspection and account remedies under UK patent practice (Designs/Patents Acts commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use and presumption against utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that an invention 'has not come into public use will raise a strong presumption against its utility' (In re Woodcrofts; In re Bakewell's; In re Allan's; In re Herbert's).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption may be rebutted by showing that (a) the nature of the invention was such that it would not likely come into immediate use (In re Jones' Patent); (b) non-user was due to the pecuniary difficulties of the patentee (In re Wright's Patent); or (c) the market for the patent was limited (In re Herbert's Patent). Strong and unanswered evidence of utility may suffice even without actual employment (In re Hughes' Patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal of extension for failure to carry into practice to benefit the public
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That the invention has not been carried into practice so as to benefit the public will also be a good ground for refusing the extension' (In re Pinkus' Patent; In re Herbert's Patent), even if delay due to disputes relating to working the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may explain the cause of delay; a reasonable excuse can lead to extension being granted (In re Norton's Patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits to be included when estimating patentee's profits for extension
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In estimating his profits, the applicant must include all profits made by him as patentee, such as result from licences or royalties, including too, profits made in another country; or made by sale for exportation' (In re Johnson's Patent; In re Hardy's Patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profits 'not as such' (e.g., manufacturing the patented article) are not included under sub-sect. 15 (see In re Betts', In re Munt's, In re Saxby's). The Committee will not go behind the accounts to apportion what part of profits is as manufacturer and what as patentee (Adair's Patent). Allowed deductions: expenses in bringing out the patent (In re Roberts'), experiments (In re Kay's), defending the patent, bringing the invention into use (In re Galloway's); a deduction for exclusive devotion of time (In re Carr's); and a manufacturer's fair profit (In re Galloway's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other circumstances considered: personal merit of the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judicial Committee will look at 'the personal merit of the inventor' distinct from public merit of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases where skill and ingenuity of the patentee in making the invention were considered include In re Daumton's, In re Whitehouse's, In re Hill's, In re Norton's. Being importer and not the inventor detracts from personal merit (In re Saames' Patent). An assignee represents the inventor's merit but the Committee may also have regard to any personal merit of the assignee (In re Galloway's; In re Morgan's; In re Whitehouse's). Prior suggestions by others do not necessarily detract from inventor's merit (In re Betts').

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of merit/utility required for extension
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A high degree of merit in the invention must be shown' and the Committee will not consider utility beyond that extent (In re Saxby's Patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On this ground the Committee refused to extend where the specification showed the subject-matter would not support a valid patent (In re McDougall's Patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prolongation on the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The Committee will consider 'the effect the prolongation might have on the public' and where prolongation would be detrimental to the public this will be taken into account (In re McInnes's Patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prolongation detrimental to public interests can be a ground for refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's willingness to grant licences on reasonable terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The willingness or unwillingness of the applicant to grant licences on reasonable terms is a factor; where an exclusive licence had been granted prolongation was refused (In re Carduell's Patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee may impose licence-related conditions or refuse extension where licence behavior is contrary to public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions the Committee may impose on extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judicial Committee 'may order the grant of a new patent, subject to any restrictions, conditions, and provisions it may think fit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of conditions imposed: securing an annuity to the original inventor (In re Whitehouse's; Russell v. Ledsam; In re Markwick's; In re Pitman's); securing a portion of profits to the original inventor or his widow (In re Hardy's; In re Herbert's); fixing sale price of patented article (In re Hardy's); granting licences to the public on certain terms (In re Mallett's); allowing the Crown liberty to use the patent without licence (In re Petit Smith's; In re Napier's) — though Privy Council sometimes refused to impose Crown-use condition (In re Carpenter's; In re Lancaster's); disclaimers of unworked portions (In re Bodmer's); securing similar licensing rights to those who previously had licence rights (In re Normandy's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and procedural requirements for petition for extension
rubrics_metrics.description: By Privy Council Rules the applicant, after advertising three times in the London Gazette and in three London papers, and three times in a country paper near where he carries on business, is 'within one week from the insertion of his last advertisement in the Gazette, to present a petition for extension.' The petition must be presented six months before patent expiry and accompanied by affidavits of the advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any person may enter a caveat and be heard; copies of the petition must be served on such person. Opposers must notify objections within one fortnight after service. Petitioner must lodge six printed copies of the specification and four copies of the balance sheet of expenditure and receipts one week before hearing; such accounts are proved at hearing. Petition must mention a day for application to fix a hearing date (not less than four weeks from last Gazette advertisement); all notices of opposition must be lodged before such day and opposers entitled to four weeks' notice of hearing. (See Form of petition in App. A.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation procedure: abolition of scire facias and revocation by petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 26 abolishes proceedings by scire facias to repeal a patent; 'Revocation of a patent may be obtained on petition to the Court.' Every ground on which a patent could be repealed by scire facias remains available as a defence to infringement and as a ground of revocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revocation petitions are to the High Court of Justice; letters patent still contain Privy Council revocation provisos. Ground types available for revocation mirror historical scire facias grounds (see sect. 29 and Form of Particulars, App. A.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may present a petition for revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for revocation may be presented by: (a) The Attorney-General in England or Ireland, or the Lord Advocate in Scotland; (b) any person authorised by those officers; (c) any person alleging the patent was obtained in fraud of his rights; (d) any person alleging he or one through whom he claims was the true inventor of any invention included in the patentee's claim; (e) any person alleging he or one through whom he claims had publicly manufactured, used, or sold within the realm, before the patent date, anything claimed by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings by scire facias formerly could be taken by anyone as illegal patents were regarded as prejudicial to the public; under the new section only persons in the listed classes have a right to present without the Attorney-General's authority; others must obtain that authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars requirement with revocation petition and amendment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The plaintiff must deliver with his petition particulars of the objections on which he means to rely, and no evidence shall, except by leave of the Court or a judge, be admitted in proof of any objection of which particulars are not so delivered.' Particulars delivered may be amended by leave of the Court or a judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particulars are essential; failure to deliver particulars prevents admission of evidence on those objections except by leave. Particulars may be amended from time to time on leave, even after trial has begun (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of defendant to begin and give evidence in revocation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The defendant shall be entitled to begin, and give evidence in support of the patent, and if the plaintiff gives evidence impeaching the validity of the patent the defendant shall be entitled to reply.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural allocation of burden and reply rights at hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for true inventor after revocation for fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent has been revoked on the ground of fraud, the Comptroller may, on application by the true inventor made in accordance with the Act, grant to him a patent in lieu of and bearing the same date as the revoked patent; but the new patent shall cease on the expiration of the term for which the revoked patent was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a limited remedy granting same-dated patent but not extending original term beyond its expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and contents of a revocation petition
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition should be addressed to the High Court of Justice and contain 'a concise statement of the material facts, but not the evidence by which it is to be proved.' It is to be divided into paragraphs and must be accompanied by particulars of objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No evidence is to be contained in the petition itself; see Williams on Petitions for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent binding the Crown and Crown's authorised use
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A patent shall have to all intents the effect as against her Majesty the Queen... as it has against a subject.' Officers administering Crown services may use the invention for Crown services on terms agreed with the patentee and approved by the Treasury, or, in default, on terms settled by the Treasury after hearing parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously letters patent did not bind the Crown; the Act alters this. The Crown may call upon the patentee to supply articles comprised in the invention at prices to be settled; failure may render the patent void (see form of patent, Form D, Sched. 1). The Crown may enforce section as soon as an application for a patent is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of assessors in patent legal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In an action or proceeding for infringement or revocation of a patent, the Court may, if it thinks fit, and shall, on the request of either of the parties to the proceeding, call in the aid of an assessor specially qualified' and try/ hear the case wholly or partially with his assistance; trial is without a jury unless Court directs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court of Appeal or Judicial Committee may also call assessors. Remuneration is determined by the Court and paid as other execution expenses. This section gives either party a right to have an assessor (except in Court of Appeal/Judicial Committee where it's discretionary). See Rules cited (Order XXXVI r.43).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery of particulars in infringement actions: timing and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) 'In an action for infringement the plaintiff must deliver with his statement of claim particulars of the breaches complained of.' (2) 'The defendant must deliver with his statement of defence particulars of any objections on which he relies.' (3) If disputing validity, particulars must state on what grounds and, for want of novelty, the time and place of the previous publication or user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No evidence at hearing shall be admitted in proof of any alleged infringement or objection of which particulars were not delivered except by leave. Particulars may be amended by leave. On taxation of costs, regard shall be had to particulars delivered; costs for particulars require Court/judge certificate they were proven or were reasonable and proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and sufficiency standard for particulars of breaches and objections
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The object of particulars of breaches is to give the defendant fair and particular notice of what the complaint is against him.' Particulars are sufficient if, taken with the pleadings, they give full notice of plaintiff's case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise pointing out of the portion of the specification infringed by reference to pages and lines is expected except in some article sales where exhibit suffices (Bailey v. Kynock). Particular parts of a machine should be pointed out. What degree of particularity depends on circumstances. Under earlier Acts prior user allegations required names/places; publications relied on must be specified with pages; drawings described sufficient for identification; specifications referred to by date and name of patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity requirements and examples for particulars of prior publication or user
rubrics_metrics.description: Where prior user by other persons is alleged, names of some such persons must be given; vague phrases like 'and other persons' may be struck out if insufficient. Places where use occurred ought to be stated, but general public user may need only reference to place where such user takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence of prior public user arises after delivery of particulars, defendant should apply to amend; after trial begins leave may be obtained on short notice (cases cited). As to prior user in a colony see relevant case law. Publications in foreign languages and pages must be specified. Drawings and patent specifications should be described to enable identification (Plimpton v. Spiller).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of particulars being too general
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Where the particulars are too general the plaintiff cannot take this objection at the trial, and any evidence within the literal meaning of the particulars will be admitted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too-general particulars may not be used to exclude evidence; parties should ensure sufficient specificity when serving particulars to avoid surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of particulars and leave rules
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Particulars of breaches or objections may be amended by leave' (sub-sect. (5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after trial begins, leave may be given to amend particulars of objection (Daw v. Hey). Effect of leave on the action depends on circumstances (see Edison Telephone Co. v. India Rubber Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and certification in respect of particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: On taxation of costs regard shall be had to particulars delivered; parties shall not be allowed costs in respect of any particular unless certified by the Court or a judge to have been proven or to have been reasonable and proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change from earlier law: certificate may be given by Court or a judge (not restricted to trial judge), and requirement is that particular was 'reasonable and proper' rather than strictly 'proved'. Certificate requirement affects entitlement to costs for particulars, and historically was necessary even in nonsuit (case law cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunction: matters plaintiff must show
rubrics_metrics.description: In applying for an interlocutory injunction the plaintiff must be prepared to show: (1) The validity of the patent; which may be shown by (a) that the patent is old and there has been active user (Plimpton v. Malcolmson), (b) that validity has been established and there is no reason to doubt the result, or (c) the defendant's conduct makes validity undoubted as against him. (2) Some actual infringement. (3) There must be no undue delay in coming to Court. (4) Where numerous infringers exist, proper course is to proceed against one and ask others to abide result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits in support must clearly set forth plaintiff's legal title and belief that at the time of making the application the patentee was the first and true inventor; the nature of alleged infringements must be particularly stated. Interlocutory injunctions will generally not be granted ex parte except in emergencies. Notice periods and motions rules apply per R.S.C. Order LI. Rule 5. The Court will consider whether the validity is sufficiently prima facie to justify an injunction (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms, conditions and remedies related to injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court has discretionary power to grant or withhold injunctions and to impose terms (e.g., undertaking by plaintiff to be liable for damages; refusal upon undertaking by defendant to keep account of profits; order to stand over until trial). Perpetual injunctions usually obtained at final trial but sometimes by consent earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunction takes form of Court Order; service requirements (before 6pm weekdays, 2pm Saturdays) and service by office copy are sufficient (R.S.C. LXXIV. r.11). Notice by telegram accepted in urgent cases. If obtaining an injunction is substantial object the writ should be endorsed accordingly. Failure to obtain interlocutory injunction does not preclude perpetual injunction but plaintiff must then establish clear and unexceptional title. Damages may be awarded in addition to or instead of injunction under Lord Cairns' Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection powers in patent litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court or Judge may, on application and on such terms as just, order inspection of any property or thing which is subject of the cause or as to which any question may arise, and may authorise entry on land or buildings, taking of samples, making observations, or trying experiments 'necessary or expedient for the purpose of obtaining full information or evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspection provisions must be read with Order L. Rule 3 of the Rules of the Supreme Court, 1883; orders may include authorising persons to enter premises and take samples or try experiments to obtain evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of profits and related orders as alternative or adjunct to injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Section empowers the Court to make orders for an injunction, inspection, or account on application of either party and impose terms and directions respecting same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may order an account of profits and may refuse injunction in favor of an undertaking to keep an account. The Court may give directions as to how accounts and inspection are to be carried out; the remedy of account is a principal equitable relief alongside injunction.
